A solar still is a device that mimics the rain cycle. It's a container that is filled
with water and allowed to sit in the sun. The sunlight evaporates the water
and forces it to condense on a glass or plastic surface. The evaporated water
condenses on this surface and becomes purified in the process. Solar stills are
commonly used for feed water. Solar Disinfection of Drinking Water
The sun is known to emit ultraviolet rays can be harmful in excessive
amounts. But, did you know that these rays are useful for treating water too? Often used in the African regions, this treatment method requires the use of
clear PET bottles (around 3 to 5 liters) as the water container.
1. Wash the PET bottle thoroughly with soap and clean water especially if
this is the first time you’ll be using it.
2. Check if the water to be treated is turbid. If it is, pre-filter the water
using cheesecloth until it becomes clear in appearance. Otherwise,
proceed to the next step.
3. Fill the PET bottle with water then leave it exposed under the sun for
six hours. If the weather is cloudy, extend the exposure of the water to
2 days.
4. Collect the solar disinfected water. You can drink it or store up to 2
days in a dark area. Keeping the disinfected water in sealed containers
reduces the risk of recontamination.

If you have a solar cooker, you can use it to pasteurize the water. Take note
that the pasteurization process will kill all forms of germs, harmful bacteria,
or disease-carrying microorganisms but it does not eliminate chemical
contamination from pesticides and industrial waste nor does it sterilize the
water. Using Heat
The final method of water purification is to simply boil it. All you need is a
pot and any kind of fuel. There aren't too many contaminants that can
withstand being boiled for longer than ten minutes or so. Unlike in chlorination where murky water needs to be pre-filtered before
treatment, boiling works well for all sorts of water (except of course heavily
polluted water). After filling the pot, allow the water to boil for several
minutes. Take note that the duration of boiling depends on the altitude. If you
live in a highly elevated area, it will take a longer time for water to boil. At
sea level, the water boils quicker due to the higher pressure exerted by the
atmosphere. As a guideline, add one more minute to your normal boiling
duration for every thousand feet above sea level. Once you are familiar with the best way to clean and purify your water, the

Every homestead has its own annual water requirement. It depends on the
number of people and the types of water-consuming activities conducted on a
daily basis, for instance, the size of your livestock or cropland influences how
much water will be used for outdoor activities. Having an idea of how much
water you need can help you verify if your current sources sufficiently meet
your demand or not. Furthermore, the annual requirement will help you
determine what the appropriate size of your water storage system is. In chapter two, you have learned a simple formula that you can use to
calculate your annual water requirement. Chapter 3 discussed all types of
water sources that you can tap in your area depending on availability. Here,
storage systems will be discussed, including how to size your tank. Types of Water Containers
Properly storing your collected and treated water is a simple process. It
entails nothing more than procuring suitable containers, sanitizing them and
making sure they are in a safe place. If a container can be sanitized and hold
water without leaking or letting in debris, it can probably be safely used to
store water. Glass jars and jugs make good containers for small amounts of water. Plastic
containers made of from materials deemed as "Food Grade" can also be used
to store water. Whether you need a small tank or a large tank, you can always
find the most suitable container for long-term storage of your non-potable
indoor water, non-potable outdoor water, and potable water. Barrels and steel drums are useful for storing large amounts of water in one
container.

Barrels and steel drums are useful for storing large amounts of water in one
container. Usually, these types of storage devices are capable of holding in
excess of fifty gallons of water. You can also use barrels as water reservoirs
for water heaters. If you need to keep a large amount of drinking water on hand, consider a
water tank. This is an investment in time, money, and requires a permanent
structure on your land but is a viable option for many situations. There are a myriad of containers available in the market to date. Each has its
own sets of advantages and disadvantages. So how do you choose the most
suitable tank? First, you need to know your storage requirement. Calculating Your Storage Requirement
For rainwater, the maximum amount you can collect will depend on three
basic factors:
1. The average precipitation in your locality;
2. The total roof catchment area; and,
3. The collection efficiency
The precipitation every year varies up to 25% either above or below the
average value. Getting at least ten years of data for rain and snow from your
local climate monitoring organization, will give you a picture of the rainfall
pattern and the estimated amount that you can collect in a particular month. The total surface area of the roof is different from the catchment area. Unlike
the surface area, the slope of your roof does not influence the catchment area.

The total surface area of the roof is different from the catchment area. Unlike
the surface area, the slope of your roof does not influence the catchment area. To determine your current catchment area, all you need to do is to measure
the following:
Width is just the distance from one gutter to the other
Length is just the total length of the gutter

Total catchment area equals width multiplied by the length
For a 9-meter wide roof that is 11 meters long, the total catchment area is:
9 times 11 = 99m2
The percentage of rainfall that lands on the roof and finds its way to your
storage is your collection efficiency. A good rule of thumb to follow is that
you can collect around 75 to 80% of the total annual precipitation. The
reasons for water loss are accounted for by the following:
Site-specific water loss due to the type of roofing material, prevailing
wind speeds, and presence of overhanging vines and branches;
Collection system loss due to overflow and spillage caused by
inefficient filters and undersized pipes; and,
Seasonal factors such as the extension of dry periods, snowfall that
remains as ice, and the need to divert water out of the collection
system due to scheduled cleaning. If this is your first time setting up a rainwater harvesting system, you can use
the annual potential rainwater collection figure to estimate your storage need. To do that, simply use the following formula:

Potential Water Collection (liters) = Total Roof Catchment Area (m2)
multiplied by Annual Precipitation (mm)
Take note that 1 mm of rain on a 1 m2 catchment area produces 1 liter of
water. Consider this example. The 12-year average annual precipitation at your local
weather station is 1,000m m. Your house has a catchment area of 90 m2.

Consider this example. The 12-year average annual precipitation at your local
weather station is 1,000m m. Your house has a catchment area of 90 m2. This
could capture:
90 m2 x 1,000 mm = 90,000 liters (90 m3) of water
If you already have existing rainwater storage and would like to know if you
need an upgrade, knowing the actual amount of rain that you can collect in a
year will give you a heads up on the size of your rainwater storage. Calculating this amount is simple using the following formula:
Actual Water Collection = Potential Water Collection multiplied by
Collection Efficiency
Going back to the previous example, if your potential water collection is
90m3, and using the rule of thumb, 75% collection efficiency, your actual
water collection is:

Actual Water Collection = 90 m3 multiplied by 0.75[3] = 67.5 m3
If you have or are planning to have an open storage facility like ponds, you
will need precipitation data for proper sizing. Your best option is to seek help
from your local Natural Resources Conservation Service conservationist to
find out how much runoff you can collect given the average precipitation
data. From this information, you can estimate the dimensions of your pond. Also, check out the water regulations implemented in your area before
proceeding with the construction and use of the pond. Storage Tank Sizing with Water Balance Tables
